title: Tailgate Drinking Guide: Pacing, Food, and Hydration Tips
excerpt: How to enjoy a tailgate without wrecking the game or your Monday: pacing a long day, what to eat, hydration in heat and cold, drinking games, and a safe ride home.
metaDescription: A 21+ tailgate drinking guide: how to pace drinks, what to eat, staying hydrated in heat or cold, drinking games, and getting home safely.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a tailgate is just a long day of drinking outdoors, usually in a parking lot, followed by a game, followed by a trip home. None of those pieces is unusual on its own. What makes tailgates rough is how they stack: an early start, a light breakfast, five or more hours before kickoff, sun or cold, drinking games, cheap cases of beer, and then three more hours inside the stadium. The people who enjoy the whole day and feel fine on Monday usually aren't drinking less heroically than everyone else. They're eating more, drinking water, spacing their drinks out, and they sorted out the ride home before they left the house.

**The quick rules:** Eat a real breakfast before the first drink, and keep eating all day. Count standard drinks, not cans or cups. Aim for about one drink an hour or slower, and decide on a rough limit while you're still sober. Alternate every drink with water. Skip or limit chugging games and shots. Dress for the weather, because alcohol makes heat and cold both more dangerous. Pick your sober driver, rideshare, or transit plan before you go. And if a friend can't be woken, is breathing slowly, or is vomiting while barely conscious, call 911 right away.

> **Who this is for, and when to get help.** This guide is general information for adults 21 and older who choose to drink at tailgates. It isn't medical advice. **Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before drinking if** you take prescription medicines (especially sedatives, sleep aids, anxiety medicines, opioids, antihistamines, or blood thinners), are pregnant or trying to get pregnant, have liver, heart, or stomach problems, or have been told to avoid alcohol. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone** can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has blue or pale skin, is having a seizure, or is vomiting while confused or passing out. Don't leave them alone to sleep it off. Roll them onto their side and stay with them until help arrives.

## Why Tailgates Hit Harder Than a Night Out

Your liver handles alcohol at roughly the same pace whether you're at a bar at 11 p.m. or in a parking lot at 11 a.m. For most people that's somewhere around one standard drink per hour, give or take. A tailgate doesn't change your biology. It changes the conditions, and almost every condition pushes in the wrong direction.

### The day is very long

A noon kickoff often means the lot opens hours earlier, and the first drink comes not long after you park. Add the game and the trip home and you can be drinking, on and off, for eight hours or more. Over that stretch, small amounts add up. Two drinks an hour sounds modest until you realize it's sixteen drinks by the final whistle. Long sessions are where people lose count, which is why we spend so much of this guide on pacing.

If you've ever noticed that afternoon drinking seems to hit differently, our guide to [day drinking](/never-hungover/day-drinking) explains why. Most of it applies here.

### Breakfast is light or missing

Early mornings and long drives mean a lot of people show up with coffee and nothing else, planning to eat once the grill is going. That first hour or two of drinking on an empty stomach is when alcohol reaches your bloodstream fastest. Food in the stomach slows the move from stomach to small intestine, which is where most alcohol gets absorbed. You can read more about that in our guide to [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach).

### Weather does its own damage

Early-season games can be hot, sunny, and humid. Late-season games can be freezing. Alcohol makes both worse. In heat, you sweat more and alcohol makes you pee more, so you can fall behind on fluids quickly. In cold, alcohol makes you feel warmer while actually letting your body lose heat faster. Both are covered in their own sections below.

### The drinks are bigger and stronger than they look

Tailgates run on cans, red cups, and coolers, and none of those come with a standard pour. A tall can of craft IPA can hold close to two standard drinks. A cup of homemade punch or "jungle juice" could hold anything. Canned cocktails and higher-alcohol seltzers vary a lot by brand. It's easy to think you've had four drinks when you've had seven.

### Then there's the game, and the ride home

Most people don't stop when they walk through the gates. Stadium drinks are expensive, which slows some people down, but others pre-load in the lot to save money. Then the game ends, everyone heads for the exits at once, and the question of who's driving comes up at the worst possible moment. That's why the ride home is the one thing worth deciding before anything else.

## Know What You're Actually Drinking

You can't pace what you can't count. In the US, one **standard drink** has about 14 grams of pure alcohol. According to the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), that's roughly:

- **12 ounces of regular beer** at about 5% alcohol
- **5 ounces of wine** at about 12%
- **1.5 ounces of 80-proof spirits** (40%), such as a shot of vodka or whiskey

Here's how common tailgate drinks compare. These are rough estimates; check the label, because strength varies widely.

| Drink | Typical size | Approximate standard drinks |
|---|---|---|
| Light beer (about 4.2%) | 12 oz can | about 0.8 |
| Regular lager (about 5%) | 12 oz can | about 1 |
| Regular lager | 16 oz tallboy | about 1.3 |
| Craft IPA (about 7%) | 16 oz can | about 1.9 |
| Hard seltzer (about 5%) | 12 oz can | about 1 |
| Higher-alcohol seltzer or canned cocktail (8% or more) | 12 oz can | 1.6 or more |
| Mixed drink in a party cup, free-poured | 16 oz cup | often 2 or more |
| Homemade punch or "jungle juice" | one cup | unknown, often high |

For a deeper breakdown, see [what counts as a standard drink](/never-hungover/what-is-a-standard-drink) and our list of [alcohol content by drink](/never-hungover/alcohol-content-by-drink).

A few counting habits that work at tailgates:

- **Bring your own drinks** so you know their strength. If you drink someone else's, read the can.
- **Treat unlabeled punch with suspicion.** You can't count it. If you have any, count each cup as at least two drinks.
- **Pour your own.** Free-poured mixed drinks are almost always bigger than you'd guess.
- **Keep a simple tally.** Some people move a bottle cap from one pocket to the other, or note it on their phone. It feels silly until you see the number.

If seltzers are your go-to, our guide to [hard seltzer hangovers](/never-hungover/hard-seltzer-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) explains why "light and refreshing" can still add up fast.

## How Much Is Too Much?

There's no single safe number for a whole tailgate, because your size, food, sleep, medications, and the length of the day all matter. But two benchmarks from US health agencies help put a long day in perspective:

- **Moderate drinking**, as described in US dietary guidance, means up to 2 drinks in a day for men and up to 1 for women. That's a day, not an hour.
- **Binge drinking**, as defined by the NIAAA, is a pattern that brings blood alcohol to about 0.08%. For a typical adult that's about **5 or more drinks for men or 4 or more for women in about two hours**.

A tailgate plus a game crosses both lines for many people without them feeling like they "went hard." That doesn't mean you have to stop at one. It means a deliberate limit beats a vague plan to "take it easy." Set a number while you're sober, tell a friend, and stick to it.

## A Tailgate Plan, Hour by Hour

The most useful thing you can do is plan the day before it starts. Here's a simple timeline you can adjust to your kickoff time.

### The night before

- **Sleep.** Showing up short on sleep makes alcohol hit harder and makes you more likely to nap in a camp chair and wake up groggy.
- **Pack water first.** Put a case of water or a few large refillable bottles in the car before you pack the beer. If it's cold out, pack a thermos for something warm and non-alcoholic.
- **Plan the ride home.** Pick the sober driver, book the rideshare pickup spot, or check the transit schedule now. More on this below.
- **Go easy the night before.** Starting a tailgate already a little hungover is a common way to feel awful by halftime.

### The morning

- **Eat a real breakfast.** Protein, some fat, and some fiber: eggs and toast, a breakfast burrito, oatmeal with nuts, Greek yogurt with fruit. Our guide to [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) goes into why this works.
- **Drink a glass or two of water** before you leave.
- **Put on sunscreen** if it's sunny, even in fall. You'll be outside for hours.

### Arriving and setting up

- **Hold off on the first drink** until you've got food going or have eaten something. If the grill takes an hour to heat up, snack on something with protein in the meantime.
- **Set up a water station** where people can see it. A separate cooler of just water and non-alcoholic drinks works well, because people grab what's in front of them.
- **Start slow.** The first hour sets the pace for the day. If the first three drinks go down in 45 minutes, catching up on water later won't fully undo it.

### The main tailgate

- **Aim for one drink an hour or slower.** On a six-hour tailgate, that alone keeps you in a very different place than the person drinking two an hour.
- **Alternate every drink with water.** This slows you down more than it hydrates you, and slowing down is the point.
- **Keep eating.** Graze through the whole tailgate, not just at one big meal.
- **Be careful with games.** Beer pong, flip cup, and shotgunning are built around drinking fast. See the section below.
- **Take breaks from drinking.** Toss a football, walk the lot, watch the pregame on someone's TV. Drinking is less automatic when your hands are busy.

### The game

- **Taper off as you head in.** Alcohol you drank in the last hour in the lot is still on its way into your blood as you go through security.
- **Many stadiums stop alcohol sales partway through the game.** Don't take that as a cue to buy two more before the cutoff.
- **Keep drinking water.** Many stadiums allow a sealed water bottle or have refill stations. Check your venue's rules before you go.

### After the game

- **Stop drinking.** Postgame drinks in the lot are what turn a good day into a bad Monday, and they're often the drinks people regret most.
- **Eat again.** A real meal after the game helps you feel better and gives the alcohol in your system time to clear before you sleep.
- **Follow your ride plan,** even if you feel fine. Feeling fine is not a reliable test.

## Food: What Actually Helps

Food doesn't absorb alcohol like a sponge, but it does slow how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream, which lowers the peak and smooths out the day. The best tailgate food has protein, some fat, and some fiber, and you eat it throughout the day rather than all at once.

**Good choices:**

- Burgers, brats, hot dogs, and grilled chicken (ideally on a bun or with sides, not alone)
- Chili, pulled pork, or anything slow-cooked and filling
- Sandwiches, wraps, and sliders
- Bean dips, guacamole, and hummus with vegetables or pita
- Wings, ideally with something besides wings
- Fruit, which also brings water

**Less helpful on their own:**

- Chips, pretzels, and popcorn. Salty snacks aren't harmful, and salt can help you hold on to fluid, but they don't fill you up and they make you thirsty. Thirst at a tailgate gets answered with beer unless water is right there.
- Sweets and desserts as the main "meal."

**A note on food safety:** tailgates are a classic setting for food poisoning, and the symptoms can be mistaken for a hangover. Keep raw meat in a separate cooler from ready-to-eat food, cook burgers and chicken all the way through, and don't leave perishable food sitting out too long. USDA guidance is not to leave perishable food out for more than 2 hours, or 1 hour when it's above 90°F. If you wake up with fever, cramps, or diarrhea, our guide to telling a [hangover from food poisoning](/never-hungover/hangover-or-food-poisoning) can help you sort out which it is.

## Hydration: Water Is the Main Tool

Alcohol makes you pee more by lowering a hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. Over a long day that adds up, and it's one of the reasons people feel drained by the second half. We cover the science in [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol).

The practical version is simple:

- **One water for every drink.** A full cup or bottle, not a sip.
- **Bring more water than you think you need.** A tailgate for six people can go through a lot of water, especially in heat.
- **Make it easy to grab.** Put water in the same cooler as the beer, on top. People drink what they reach first.
- **Electrolytes are optional, not magic.** If you're sweating a lot in heat, an electrolyte drink or a salty snack with water can help you replace what you lose. On a mild day, plain water does most of the job.
- **Check the color.** Pale yellow urine is a reasonable sign you're keeping up. Dark yellow means drink more water now.

Water won't prevent intoxication or stop a hangover by itself, since dehydration is only one part of what causes a hangover. But it slows your drinking, keeps you steadier through a long day, and makes the next morning easier. For the morning after, see [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking).

## Weather: Heat and Cold Both Get More Dangerous

### Hot-weather games

Sun, heat, and alcohol are a rough combination. You lose fluid through sweat while alcohol increases how much you lose through urine, and alcohol can make it harder to notice that you're overheating.

- Drink extra water and find shade, especially from late morning through mid-afternoon.
- Wear sunscreen, a hat, and light clothing. A sunburn on top of a hangover is miserable.
- Slow your drinking on hot days rather than speeding it up because cold beer feels refreshing.
- **Know the warning signs of heat illness:** heavy sweating, cold or clammy skin, dizziness, nausea, headache, and weakness can point to heat exhaustion. Move to a cool place, loosen clothing, and sip water. Confusion, a very high body temperature, hot skin, or passing out can mean heatstroke, which is a medical emergency. Call 911.

Our [summer drinking safety guide](/never-hungover/summer-alcohol-consumption-dhm-safety-guide) has more on drinking in the heat.

### Cold-weather games

Late-season games bring the opposite problem, and it's sneakier. Alcohol widens blood vessels near your skin, which sends warm blood to the surface and makes you feel warm. But that's exactly how your body loses heat, so your core temperature can actually drop faster. Alcohol also dulls your sense of how cold you are and can blunt shivering. We explain the mechanism in [why alcohol makes you feel warm](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-feel-warm).

- Dress in layers, and cover your head, hands, and feet.
- Bring something warm and non-alcoholic, like hot chocolate, cider, or coffee, and alternate it with drinks.
- You'll feel less thirsty in the cold, so drink water on a schedule.
- Watch friends who have been drinking. **Signs of hypothermia** include intense shivering (or shivering that stops while the person is still cold), slurred speech, clumsiness, confusion, and drowsiness. These overlap with being drunk, which is what makes them easy to miss. Get the person somewhere warm and call 911 if they seem confused or very drowsy.
- Don't let anyone "sleep it off" alone in a cold car or outside.

## Drinking Games, Shotguns, and Shots

Beer pong, flip cup, and shotgunning are part of tailgate culture, and plenty of people enjoy them. The problem is that they're designed to make you drink fast and keep you from counting.

- **A shotgunned beer is still a full drink.** You're just getting all of it at once instead of over 20 or 30 minutes, which spikes your blood alcohol faster.
- **Games make it easy to stack drinks before the first ones hit.** Alcohol keeps rising in your blood for a while after you stop drinking, so you can feel fine at the end of a game and much drunker 30 minutes later.
- **If you play, play with less.** Use light beer, fill cups partway, or play with water and treat the cups as points. Nobody will notice.
- **Shots are the fastest way to lose the thread.** If you take one, count it as a full drink and drink water right after.

Our [party drinking tips](/never-hungover/party-drinking-tips) guide has more on pacing when everyone around you is going faster, including how to turn down a drink without making it a thing.

## Getting Home Safely

This is the most important section of the guide. Most of the serious harm on big game days comes from impaired driving, and stadium traffic means a lot of cars, a lot of pedestrians, and a lot of people who've been drinking all day.

- **Decide before you drink.** Who's driving, or how are you getting home? Make the call while everyone's sober.
- **A designated driver means zero drinks, not "a few early."** Make sure your driver has plenty of good food and non-alcoholic drinks, and thank them.
- **Rideshares and transit** are good options, but stadium pickups can take a long time. Agree on a meeting spot away from the gates, and keep your phone charged.
- **Don't sleep it off in the driver's seat.** In many states you can be charged with impaired driving if you're in the driver's seat with access to the keys, even if the car is parked.
- **"I feel fine" isn't a test.** Only time lowers your blood alcohol. Coffee, food, water, and cold air don't speed it up. See [how long after drinking you can drive](/never-hungover/how-long-after-drinking-can-you-drive) for more.
- **Walking home is a risk too.** Drunk pedestrians in busy traffic are at real risk. Walk with friends, stay on sidewalks, and cross at lights.

## Looking Out for Each Other

At a big tailgate, it's easy to assume someone else is keeping an eye on the friend who's had too much. Make it you. Know the signs of alcohol poisoning:

- Confusion or stupor
- Vomiting, especially while drowsy or confused
- Slow breathing (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute) or long gaps between breaths
- Seizures
- Pale, blue, or cold, clammy skin
- Can't be woken up

If you see these, **call 911.** Don't wait for every sign. Keep the person on their side so they won't choke if they vomit, and stay with them. Don't give them coffee or a cold shower, and don't let them sleep it off alone in a car or a tent. Our full guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) explains what to do while you wait.

## If You're Hosting the Tailgate

The host has more influence over how the day goes than anyone else. A few small choices make a big difference:

- **Feed people early.** Get food out before most people are on their second drink.
- **Make water impossible to miss.** A dedicated water cooler, or water on top of the beer.
- **Have good non-alcoholic options.** Non-alcoholic beer, sparkling water, soda, and warm drinks in cold weather. Some guests will be designated drivers, some won't want to drink, and some will want a break.
- **Label anything homemade.** If you make a punch, tell people roughly how strong it is.
- **Don't push drinks.** Offering is fine. Insisting isn't.
- **Keep an eye on the end of the day.** Help guests sort out rides, and don't hand anyone their keys if they've been drinking.
- **This is a 21+ activity.** College tailgates in particular mix ages. Don't serve anyone under the legal drinking age, and know that hosts can face legal consequences for doing so.

## Who Should Skip Alcohol at the Tailgate

You can enjoy every part of a tailgate without drinking. Skipping alcohol is the right call if you:

- **Are driving.**
- **Take medicines that interact with alcohol**, such as sedatives, sleep aids, anxiety medicines, opioid pain relievers, some antidepressants, or certain antibiotics. Ask your doctor or pharmacist whether alcohol is safe with what you take.
- **Are pregnant or trying to get pregnant.**
- **Have liver disease, a heart condition, or a stomach condition** your doctor has told you alcohol worsens.
- **Are under 21.**

If you notice that tailgates have become hard to enjoy without drinking a lot, or that you often drink more than you planned, that's worth a conversation with a doctor. You don't need to wait for a crisis.

## The Next Morning

If you followed the plan, Monday should be manageable. If you didn't, here's the short list:

- **Drink water** steadily through the morning, and add an electrolyte drink if you're queasy or sweated a lot.
- **Eat something gentle** with carbs and some protein, like toast with eggs, a banana, or soup.
- **Rest.** Sleep is one of the few things that reliably helps, since alcohol disrupts sleep quality even when it helps you fall asleep.
- **Be careful with painkillers.** Don't stack acetaminophen (Tylenol) on a heavy drinking day, and take ibuprofen or naproxen only with food. See our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol).
- **Don't drive** if you drank late into the night. You might still be over the legal limit in the morning.

The Monday after a big game has its own reputation, and our guide to the [Super Bowl Monday hangover](/never-hungover/super-bowl-monday-hangover) covers how to get through a workday after one. For more general advice, see [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover). Big game days often show up on lists of the [biggest drinking days of the year](/never-hungover/biggest-drinking-days-of-the-year), and the same plan works for all of them.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound sold as a hangover supplement. Early research, mostly in animals and cells, suggests it may affect how the body processes alcohol and may support the liver, but human evidence is limited. There's no good evidence that it lowers your blood alcohol, keeps you from getting drunk, or makes it safe to drive.

If you want to try it, treat it as a possible small extra, not a replacement for food, water, pacing, and sleep. Two well-reviewed options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). See our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) for how people typically take it, and talk to your doctor first if you take any prescription medicines.

## The Bottom Line

A good tailgate is a long, social, outdoor day, and the habits that make it go well are simple. Eat before you drink and keep eating. Count standard drinks, not cans. Go about one drink an hour or slower, with water in between. Respect the weather. Go easy on the games. And settle the ride home before the first beer. Do those things and you'll actually remember the game, enjoy the drive home, and show up on Monday in decent shape.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How many drinks is too many at a tailgate?**

There's no number that's safe for everyone, because body size, food, medications, and hours all matter. A useful frame: US dietary guidance describes moderate drinking as up to 2 drinks a day for men and 1 for women, and the NIAAA defines binge drinking as about 5 or more drinks for men or 4 or more for women in roughly two hours. A tailgate plus a game can easily pass those lines without anyone noticing, so set a rough limit before the first drink and count standard drinks, not cans.

**What should I eat before a tailgate?**

Eat a real meal with protein, some fat, and fiber before the first drink, such as eggs and toast, a breakfast burrito, or yogurt with oats and nuts. Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream. Then keep eating through the tailgate: burgers, brats, chicken, chili, and sandwiches all help. Chips and dip alone don't do much.

**How do I stay hydrated at a tailgate?**

Alternate every alcoholic drink with a full cup or bottle of water, bring more water than you think you need, and keep it somewhere you can see it. In heat, drink extra and get shade. In cold weather, you'll feel less thirsty, so drink water on a schedule anyway. An electrolyte drink can help if you're sweating a lot, but plain water does most of the work.

**Does drinking keep you warm at a cold-weather game?**

No. Alcohol makes you feel warmer because it widens blood vessels near your skin, but that same effect lets your core lose heat faster. It also dulls your sense of how cold you actually are. At a cold game, dress in layers, keep your head and hands covered, drink something warm and non-alcoholic, and watch friends who have been drinking for signs of shivering, clumsiness, or confusion.

**Can I sleep it off in my car after the game?**

It's risky legally and not as safe as it sounds. In many US states you can be charged with impaired driving if you're in the driver's seat with access to the keys, even if the car is parked. Alcohol also keeps rising in your blood for a while after your last drink. The safest plan is a sober designated driver, a rideshare, or transit, decided before you start drinking.

**Is shotgunning a beer worse than drinking it normally?**

It's the same amount of alcohol, but you take it in all at once instead of over 20 to 30 minutes. That spikes your blood alcohol faster and makes it easy to stack drinks before the first one has hit. Drinking games that involve chugging have the same problem. If you join in, count each one as a full drink and slow down afterward.

**Does DHM help with tailgate hangovers?**

DHM (dihydromyricetin) has interesting early research on alcohol metabolism, mostly in animals, and human evidence is limited. There's no good evidence that it lowers blood alcohol, prevents intoxication, or makes it safe to drive. If you try it, treat it as a possible small extra alongside the basics that work: food, water, pacing, and sleep.
